newsitem.title: INDIA: Weizman asks India to free jailed Israelis.
newsitem.headline: Weizman asks India to free jailed Israelis.

text.p: Israeli President Ezer Weizman watched the signing of four agreements with India on Monday but officials said he spent more time trying to persuade his hosts to free six Israelis jailed by New Delhi in drug-related cases.

"The issue was raised but we don't want to comment on it publicly because it could spoil things," one official close to the talks between Weizman and Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda told Reuters.
Weizman took the same line later at a news conference saying only that the issue involved "five fellows and a lady".
Officials had earlier said there were seven Israeli prisoners being held in India on drug charges.
They said two of the Israelis were sentenced to 10 years in prison earlier this month for peddling drugs. The charges against the other four were not immediately known.
Many young Israelis visiting India each year are believed to experiment with drugs, including heroin and hashish, both easily available in the country despite an official ban, officials said.

On the second day of his first visit to New Delhi, Weizman was accorded a colourful ceremonial welcome at the British-built Presidential Palace although the booming 21-gun salute triggered a minor panic in his delegation.
"In Israel we use rifle shots, not field cannons to welcome state guests," an Israeli official said. "Loud booms make Israelis very tense. They have a different connotation for us."
The four agreements signed by officials of the two countries were aimed at boosting cooperation in agricultural reasearch and scientific and cultural exchanges.
Weizman earlier said he felt terrific about his visit to India, saying both countries shared a common legacy of British rule and their fight for independence from colonialism.

Weizman was asked to compare his past as a British air force pilot in India in 1946 with his Indian host President Shankar Dayal Sharma, who campaigned non-violently against British rule at that time.
Weizman said: "You had the more difficult battle because you had them here for 200 years. We had them only for 30 years.
"Thank God both of us are independent now. You did it before us in 1947. It took us another year. But this is one common ground we have. The British and independence," he said.
"I feel terrific to be back here after 51 years," Weizman said.
Indian diplomats said Weizman's visit would focus on more than 100 joint ventures between Israel and India, most of them in agriculture, irrigation and water conservation.
His visit marks a high in relations that have strengthened since India established diplomatic ties with Israel in 1992 after decades of Cold War suspicions linked to the Palestinian problem.
